definition: Anything a function does that can be observed outside it apart from returning a value: printing, writing a file or database, changing a global or one of its arguments, or throwing an exception to the caller.
example: A function that appends to a log file every time it is called has a side effect.

definition: A function that always returns the same output for the same inputs. Being deterministic is only half of purity: a deterministic function can still have side effects such as logging.
example: def f(x): print(x); return x is deterministic but not pure.

definition: A design pattern, popularised by Gary Bernhardt, in which the decision-making logic is written as pure functions over plain data (the core) and a thin outer layer does all the I/O (the shell). The core can then be tested without mocks.
example: The shell reads today's date and the order from the database, passes them to a pure apply_discount function, and saves the result.

definition: A variable name that cannot be pointed at a different value after it is set, such as JavaScript const or Java final. The value it refers to can still be changed if that value is mutable.
example: const xs = [1, 2]; xs.push(3) works, but xs = [] throws a TypeError.

definition: An object whose contents cannot be changed after creation, as opposed to a name that cannot be rebound. Tuples, strings and frozensets in Python are immutable values.
example: Python strings are immutable values: "abc".upper() returns a new string rather than changing the old one.

definition: Immutability that extends all the way down: neither the object nor anything reachable from it can be changed. It needs immutable types at every level, or a deep-freeze routine or library.
example: (1, (2, 3)) is deeply immutable; (1, [2, 3]) is not.

definition: Changing a value in place, so that everyone holding a reference to it sees the change. Functional programming avoids mutation that is visible outside a function.
example: list.append mutates the list; [*xs, x] builds a new one instead.

definition: A variable defined at module or program level that any function can read or, if allowed, change. Reading a global that can change makes a function impure.
example: A COUNT variable at the top of a Python module, updated with global COUNT inside a function.

definition: A fake stand-in for a real dependency, such as a database or clock, used in tests so the code under test does not do real I/O. Pure functions need no mocks because all their inputs are arguments.
example: Patching date.today() to return 1 January in a test is a mock.

definition: Running several computations at the same time, for example on different CPU cores. Pure functions with no shared mutable state can run in parallel without locks.
example: Mapping a pure function over 1,000 images on 8 cores at once.

definition: A mechanism that lets only one thread at a time enter a section of code or touch some data, preventing data races. Immutable data needs no locks for reading.
example: A mutex around a shared counter is a lock.

definition: A Python decorator in the functools module that memoises a function: it stores results keyed by the arguments and returns the stored result on a repeat call. By default it keeps the 128 most recently used results; arguments must be hashable.
example: @lru_cache on a recursive fib function makes fib(100) instant.

definition: A Python decorator (since Python 3.9) that memoises a function with an unbounded cache: the same as lru_cache(maxsize=None).
example: With @functools.cache, the body of fib(k) runs once for each distinct k.

definition: In Python, an object that has a hash value that never changes during its lifetime and can be compared for equality, so it can be a dictionary key or set member. Built-in mutable containers such as lists and dicts are unhashable.
example: hash((1, 2)) works; hash([1, 2]) raises TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'.

definition: GHC's interactive environment, a read-eval-print loop for Haskell. Code typed into it is normally interpreted without optimisation, so space leaks that optimised code avoids can show up there.
example: Typing foldl (+) 0 [1..10^8] into GHCi can use gigabytes of memory.

definition: A compiler optimisation that computes a repeated expression once and reuses the result. It is only safe when the expression is pure, because otherwise the repeated calls might do different things.
example: f(x) + f(x) can become let y = f(x) in y + y when f is pure.

definition: The Python exception raised when code tries to assign to a field of a frozen dataclass instance.
example: a.age = 40 on a frozen User raises FrozenInstanceError.

definition: JavaScript's ... syntax, which copies the elements of an array or the properties of an object into a new array or object. It is the usual way to make an updated copy without mutating the original. The copy is shallow.
example: { ...a, age: 37 } copies a and overrides age.

definition: A JavaScript declaration that creates an immutable binding: the name can't be reassigned, but an object or array it refers to can still be changed.
example: const xs = [1]; xs.push(2) is allowed; xs = [] throws TypeError.

definition: An opt-in restricted variant of JavaScript, turned on with "use strict" and automatically in modules and classes. Among other things, it turns silent failures, such as writing to a frozen property, into thrown errors.
example: In strict mode, cfg.port = 2 on a frozen cfg throws TypeError instead of being ignored.

definition: The informal name for ordinary JavaScript that is not in strict mode. Some invalid operations, such as assigning to a read-only property, fail silently there instead of throwing.
example: In a sloppy-mode script, writing to a frozen object's property is silently ignored.

definition: A JavaScript library of persistent immutable collections (List, Map, Set and others) built on tries and hash array mapped tries, so updates return new versions that share structure with the old ones.
example: map2 = map1.set("b", 50) leaves map1 unchanged.

definition: A JavaScript library that lets you write ordinary mutating code against a temporary draft object; it then produces a new immutable object that shares every untouched part with the original. Redux Toolkit uses it.
example: produce(state, d => { d.todos.push(t) }) returns new state without changing the old one.

definition: The 2025 edition of the JavaScript standard. It added iterator helper methods such as map, filter, take and drop on Iterator.prototype, which work lazily.
example: naturals().filter(isEven).take(3) yields 2, 4, 6 without building an array.

definition: A garbage-collection design that splits the heap by object age and collects the young area often. Most objects die young, so short-lived values created by immutable updates are cheap to reclaim.
example: The JVM, .NET and V8 all use generational collectors.

definition: A divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that picks a pivot and partitions the array around it, then sorts each side. Its usual form swaps elements in place, which is natural in imperative code.
example: Sorting [3, 1, 2] with pivot 2 partitions it into [1], [2], [3].

definition: A data structure that tracks which items belong to which group and can merge groups quickly. Its efficient form updates parent pointers in place, so it fits imperative code best.
example: Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm uses union-find to check whether two nodes are already connected.

definition: A graph representation that stores, for each node, an array of its neighbours. Graph algorithms usually update such arrays or visited flags in place.
example: Node 0 → [1, 2] means node 0 has edges to nodes 1 and 2.

definition: A mutable variable in Haskell's IO monad. Reading and writing it are IO actions, so mutation is explicit in the types.
example: newIORef 0 creates a counter that modifyIORef can increment.

definition: A mutable variable used inside Haskell's ST monad. Its type ties it to one runST computation, so the mutation can't be observed from outside.
example: An STRef can hold a running total inside a runST block.

definition: A JavaScript library for building user interfaces from components. It decides whether to re-render by comparing old and new state and props by reference, so updates must create new objects rather than mutate old ones.
example: Returning the same mutated object from a reducer can make React skip the re-render.

definition: A React hook that manages state through a reducer function (state, action) → next state. React compares the next state with the previous one using Object.is, so a reducer must return a new object to signal a change.
example: const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, { todos: [] }).

definition: A JavaScript library for managing application state as one immutable object updated by reducers. React-Redux connects it to React; Redux Toolkit is the recommended way to write it and uses Immer.
example: dispatch({ type: "add", todo }) runs the reducer to produce the next state.

definition: A React-Redux hook that reads a value from the Redux store. By default it re-renders the component only when the selected value changes by strict reference equality (===).
example: useSelector(s => s.items) does not re-render if items was mutated in place.

definition: A JavaScript function that tells whether two values are the same value. For objects it compares identity (the same object in memory), not contents. React uses it to compare state.
example: Object.is(a, a) is true; Object.is({}, {}) is false.

definition: A React function that wraps a component so it skips re-rendering when each of its props is the same, compared with Object.is, as last time.
example: React.memo(Row) skips re-rendering a row whose props object fields are all unchanged references.

definition: Comparing two values by whether they are the very same object in memory, rather than by their contents. It is O(1), and with immutable data a different reference reliably signals a change.
example: In JavaScript, [1] === [1] is false because they are two different arrays.

definition: Random number generator: code or hardware that produces random-looking numbers. A software RNG keeps hidden internal state that advances on each call, so functions that use it are impure.
example: random.random() in Python reads and advances the module's RNG state.

definition: Stock keeping unit: a retailer's code identifying one specific product variant.
example: A blue T-shirt in size M might have the SKU TS-BLU-M.

definition: Foreign exchange rate: the price of one currency in another. It changes continually, so a function that reads a live FX rate is not pure.
example: An FX rate of 1.17 means 1 pound buys 1.17 euros.

definition: Short for database: an organised store of data that programs read and write. Reading or writing a DB is I/O, so it belongs in the imperative shell.
example: db.load(order_id) reads an order from the DB.

definition: Cached data that no longer matches the current source, because the source changed after the result was stored. Caching an impure function produces stale results.
example: A price cached at 9 am is stale after the 10 am price update.

definition: A language has first-class functions when functions are ordinary values: they can be stored in variables and lists, passed as arguments and returned from other functions.
example: In Python, ops = [len, str.upper] stores two functions in a list.

definition: The higher-order function map(f, xs), which applies f to every element of a collection and returns the results, one per element and in the same order. For a functor, map applies f to whatever is inside the box.
The higher-order function filter(p, xs), which keeps the elements for which the predicate p returns true, unchanged and in order. Its output is never longer than its input.
example: filter(lambda x: x > 2, [1, 3, 5]) gives 3 and 5.

definition: A higher-order function that combines all the elements of a list into one value by repeatedly applying a combining function to an accumulator and the next element, starting from an initial value. map and filter can both be written as folds.
example: reduce(add, [1, 2, 3, 4], 0) gives 10.

definition: Haskell's left fold: foldl f z [a, b, c] computes f (f (f z a) b) c, combining from the left with the initial value first. It is tail-recursive, but its lazy accumulator can build a long chain of thunks.
Haskell's strict left fold from Data.List. It forces the accumulator to weak head normal form at every step with seq, so summing a long list keeps a plain number instead of a chain of thunks.
example: foldl' (+) 0 [1..10^7] runs in constant accumulator space.

definition: Haskell's right fold: foldr f z [a, b, c] computes f a (f b (f c z)), combining from the right with the initial value last. It is the natural fold for building lists and works on infinite lists when f doesn't need its second argument.
A variable or parameter that carries a running partial result through a loop, fold or recursion, such as a running total. Passing it forward is what makes many recursive functions tail-recursive.
example: In reduce(add, [1, 2, 3], 0) the accumulator goes 0, 1, 3, 6.

definition: The starting value of something before any steps run. In a fold it is the starting value of the accumulator: choosing the operation's identity (0 for addition, 1 for multiplication, an empty list for concatenation) makes an empty input return a sensible result.
example: [].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) returns 0 instead of throwing.

definition: A small function written inline without a name. Python writes lambda x: x * 2, JavaScript x => x * 2, Haskell \x -> x * 2, and maths λx. x × 2, where λ is the Greek letter lambda.
example: sorted(words, key=lambda w: len(w)) sorts words by length.

definition: JavaScript's compact function syntax, (args) => expression. Nested arrow functions such as a => b => a + b give curried functions.
example: xs.map(x => x * x) squares each element.

definition: An object that produces the elements of a sequence one at a time on request. Iterators are usually one-shot: once consumed, they produce nothing more.
example: In Python 3, map(f, xs) returns an iterator; list() on it a second time gives [].

definition: An iterator that can be traversed only once. After it has produced all its values it is exhausted, and iterating again silently yields nothing.
example: sum(gen) followed by sum(gen) gives 14 and then 0 for a generator of 0, 1, 4, 9.

definition: A closure that looks up a captured variable's value when it is called, not when it was created. In a loop, every closure then sees the variable's final value.
example: [lambda: i for i in range(3)] gives three functions that all return 2.

definition: The region of a program in which a name refers to a particular variable. A closure keeps access to the variables of the scope it was defined in.
example: Each call to make_multiplier(n) creates a new scope with its own n.

definition: Said of an operator that groups from the right when chained: a → b → c means a → (b → c). Haskell's function-type arrow is right-associative, which is why curried types read naturally.
example: Int -> Int -> Int means Int -> (Int -> Int).

definition: Building a new function by feeding the output of one function into another: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)), read "f after g". Haskell writes f . g.
example: (show . length . words) "to be or not" gives "4".

definition: The small circle ∘ used in maths for function composition: f ∘ g is the function that applies g, then f. Haskell uses a full stop for the same thing.
example: If g adds 1 and f doubles, (f ∘ g)(5) = 12.

definition: The | operator in a Unix shell, which feeds one program's output into the next program's input, composing small tools into a pipeline.
example: cat log | grep ERR | wc -l counts the error lines in a log.

definition: A chain of processing steps where each step's output is the next step's input, such as filter, then map, then reduce.
example: xs.filter(isEven).map(square).reduce(add, 0) is a three-step pipeline.

definition: The base of a number system: 10 for decimal, 2 for binary, 16 for hexadecimal. JavaScript's parseInt takes it as an optional second argument, from 2 to 36.
example: parseInt("10", 2) reads "10" in radix 2 and returns 2.

definition: A JavaScript function, parseInt(string, radix), that parses a string as an integer in the given base. A radix of 0 or undefined means "work it out", usually decimal; 1 or values above 36 give NaN.
example: ["1", "2", "3"].map(parseInt) gives [1, NaN, NaN] because map passes the index as the radix.

definition: Not a Number: a special floating-point value that represents an undefined or unrepresentable numeric result. JavaScript returns it from failed numeric parsing.
example: parseInt("3", 2) is NaN because 3 is not a binary digit.

definition: Python syntax for building a list from an iterable with an expression and optional for and if clauses, such as [x * x for x in xs if x % 2 == 0]. A comprehension with two for clauses is a flat_map.
example: [(x, y) for x in [1, 2] for y in "ab"] gives four pairs.

definition: A temporary collection created by one step of a pipeline only to be consumed by the next. Each filter or map call on a JavaScript array allocates one.
example: xs.filter(f).map(g) builds an intermediate array holding the filtered elements.

definition: A function passed to another function to be called later, such as the function given to map or to an event handler.
example: In arr.map(x => x * 2), x => x * 2 is the callback.

definition: A function that returns a result for every possible input, never throwing or looping forever. A partial function fails on some inputs.
example: x => x * 2 is total on numbers; x => 1 / x is not total for integers in Python, which raises on 0.

definition: The part of a recursive function that breaks the input into a smaller piece, calls itself on it and combines the result.
example: length(xs) = 1 + length(xs[1:]) is the recursive case.

definition: Choosing what code to run by matching a value against shapes, and naming its parts at the same time. In Haskell, [] matches an empty list and (x:xs) a list with head x and tail xs.
example: length' [] = 0 and length' (_:xs) = 1 + length' xs are two pattern-matching cases.

definition: A quantity, such as a list's length or a counter, that decreases with every recursive call and can't decrease forever. Finding one proves that a recursion terminates.
example: The argument n in countdown(n - 1) for n ≥ 0 is a well-founded measure.

definition: A program or function terminates when it is guaranteed to finish rather than run forever. Recursion terminates when every call makes progress towards a base case.
example: countdown(n - 2) from 5 never terminates because it skips the base case 0.

definition: Recursion that only calls itself on parts of its input, such as the tail of a list or the children of a tree node. Because the data is finite, it is guaranteed to terminate.
example: Summing a tree by summing its children's subtrees is structural recursion.

definition: The region of memory where a program keeps one frame for each function call that hasn't finished yet. It is much smaller than the heap, so deep recursion can exhaust it.
example: A recursion 1,000 calls deep keeps 1,000 frames on the call stack.

definition: A stack data structure (such as a Python list) that a loop manages itself to hold pending work, replacing the call stack used by recursion.
example: stack = [root]; while stack: node = stack.pop() walks a tree without recursion.

definition: A cap on how deep recursion may go. CPython's default is usually 1,000 frames, read with sys.getrecursionlimit() and changed with sys.setrecursionlimit().
example: A tail-recursive sum over 50,000 numbers fails in CPython because 50,000 > 1,000.

definition: A JavaScript error for a value outside its allowed range; engines also throw it when the call stack size is exceeded.
example: RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded.

definition: The machine-level call stack that the C code of an interpreter such as CPython runs on. It is separate from Python's own count of frames and has a fixed size set by the operating system.
example: Raising Python's recursion limit too far can overflow the C stack and crash the process.

definition: The JavaScript engine in Apple's WebKit, used by Safari. WebKit has documented support for ES2015 proper tail calls in strict mode.
example: Safari runs page scripts on JavaScriptCore.

definition: Recursion in which the recursive call is a tail call. With tail call elimination it runs in constant stack space, exactly like a loop.
example: sumTo acc n = sumTo (acc + n) (n - 1) is tail-recursive.

definition: Reusing the current stack frame for a tail call instead of pushing a new one, so tail-recursive code runs in constant stack space. Scheme guarantees it; CPython and V8 do not do it.
example: With TCO, a tail-recursive loop of a million iterations uses one frame.

definition: A technique for deep recursion without tail call optimisation: each step returns a thunk describing the next step instead of calling it, and a driver loop keeps calling thunks until it gets a real value.
example: run(even)(1e6) finishes with true instead of overflowing the stack.

definition: Two or more functions that call each other in a cycle.
example: isEven(n) calls isOdd(n - 1), which calls isEven(n - 2).

definition: The sequence 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ..., where each number after the first two is the sum of the two before it. Naive recursion on it makes exponentially many calls.
The number φ (phi) = (1 + √5) / 2 ≈ 1.618. Consecutive Fibonacci numbers grow by about this factor, so naive Fibonacci recursion makes about 1.6 times more calls for each step up in n.
A closed-form expression for the n-th Fibonacci number: F(n) = (φ^n − ψ^n) / √5, where φ ≈ 1.618 is the golden ratio and ψ = 1 − φ ≈ −0.618. For large n, F(n) is very close to φ^n / √5.
An equation that defines each term of a sequence using earlier terms, such as F(n) = F(n − 1) + F(n − 2). Counting the calls of a recursive function usually gives one.
example: C(n) = 1 + C(n − 1) + C(n − 2) counts the calls of naive fib.

definition: A formula that computes a value directly with a fixed number of standard operations, without recursion or a loop over all earlier terms.
example: n × (n − 1) / 2 is the closed form of 0 + 1 + ... + (n − 1).

definition: A running time that multiplies by a constant factor every time the input grows by one, such as about 1.6^n calls for naive Fibonacci. It becomes impractical even for modest inputs.
example: Naive fib(30) makes about 2.7 million calls; fib(40) about 330 million.

definition: A simplifying assumption in algorithm analysis that every arithmetic operation takes the same constant time, however large the numbers. Real big integers cost more as they grow.
example: Under the unit-cost model, adding two 1,000-digit numbers counts as one step.

definition: A minimalist dialect of Lisp whose standard requires proper tail calls, so tail-recursive loops always run in constant space.
example: (define (loop n) (if (= n 0) 'done (loop (- n 1)))) runs in constant space for any n.

definition: The virtual machine that runs Erlang and Elixir. It eliminates tail calls, so tail-recursive process loops can run forever.
example: A GenServer running for months on the BEAM is a tail-recursive loop.

definition: A standard Erlang/Elixir building block for a long-running server process that keeps state and handles messages in a loop.
example: A GenServer can hold a counter and reply with its value on request.

definition: A Clojure special form that jumps back to the start of the enclosing function or loop with new arguments, without growing the stack. The compiler rejects it if it is not in tail position.
example: (loop [i 0] (if (< i 10) (recur (inc i)) i)) returns 10.

definition: A tree in which every node has at most one child, so it is really a linked list and its height equals its number of nodes.
example: Inserting 1, 2, 3, 4 into an unbalanced binary search tree gives a degenerate tree of height 4.

definition: A compiler analysis that works out which values a function will definitely need, so a lazy language can evaluate them eagerly and avoid building thunks.
example: With -O, GHC's strictness analysis often turns foldl (+) 0 xs on Int into a tight loop.

definition: An integer type whose size grows as needed, limited only by memory, such as Python's int and Haskell's Integer. Arithmetic on very large values takes longer than on fixed-size machine integers.
example: 2 ** 100 in Python gives the exact 31-digit result.

definition: A fixed-size integer that fits in a processor register, such as a 64-bit Int in Haskell. Arithmetic on it is fast, but it can overflow.
example: Haskell's Int is 64 bits on 64-bit machines.

definition: The IEEE 754 64-bit floating-point format used for JavaScript numbers. It represents all integers exactly up to 2^53.
example: 1e6 is exactly 1,000,000 in binary64.

definition: JavaScript's arbitrary-precision integer type, separate from ordinary numbers and written with an n suffix.
example: 2n ** 100n gives an exact 31-digit BigInt.

definition: The evaluation strategy where a function's arguments are fully evaluated before the function runs (call-by-value). Most languages, including Python and JavaScript, are strict.
example: In f(g(x)), g(x) runs first even if f never uses it.

definition: The evaluation strategy where an expression is computed only when its value is needed, and at most once, with the result shared (call-by-need). Haskell uses it by default.
example: let y = expensive 42 in 0 never runs expensive.

definition: Any evaluation strategy in which an argument need not be evaluated before a function is called, so a function can return a result even if an unused argument would fail or loop forever. Call-by-name and call-by-need are non-strict.
example: In Haskell, const 1 undefined returns 1 without touching undefined.

definition: A non-strict evaluation strategy that passes an argument unevaluated and re-evaluates it every time it is used. It can repeat expensive work.
example: With call-by-name, y + y evaluates the expression bound to y twice.

definition: A delayed computation: an object that remembers how to compute a value, and the variables it needs, without having computed it yet. Under call-by-need it is replaced by its value the first time it is forced.
example: lambda: slow_query() in Python is a hand-made thunk.

aliases: forced to weak head normal form
definition: Making a lazy value actually compute, for example because its result is needed or because seq demands it.
example: Printing a lazy list forces each element it shows.

definition: A structure, such as the list of all natural numbers, that is conceptually endless but usable under lazy evaluation because only the parts actually examined are ever built.
Code that generates values for other code to use. In a lazy pipeline the producer can describe every candidate value while a separate consumer decides how many to take.
example: iterate improve guess is a producer of ever-better approximations.

definition: Code that takes values from a producer and uses them, deciding how much to ask for. In a lazy pipeline, costs appear where the consumer demands values.
example: take 3 is a consumer that asks for exactly three elements.

definition: A 1984/1990 paper by John Hughes arguing that higher-order functions and lazy evaluation are the real strengths of functional programming, because they let programs be built from separately written, reusable pieces.
example: Its numerical examples separate a producer of approximations from a consumer that stops when close enough.

definition: A function that produces a sequence of values lazily, pausing at each yield and resuming when the next value is requested. Python marks one by using yield; JavaScript with function*.
example: def naturals(): n = 1; while True: yield n; n += 1 generates 1, 2, 3, ... forever.

definition: Python syntax like a list comprehension but with round brackets, (x * x for x in xs), which creates a lazy generator instead of building a list.
example: sum(x * x for x in range(10**6)) never stores a million squares.

definition: The keyword that makes a function a generator: yield value hands one value to the caller and pauses until the next one is requested. yield from delegates to another iterable.
example: yield from (l.strip() for l in f) keeps the file open until the caller finishes.

definition: Python's standard module of fast iterator building blocks, such as islice (take a slice lazily), product, cycle and tee. Some of them buffer or cache input, so they are not all memory-free.
example: list(islice(naturals(), 5)) gives [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].

definition: To turn a lazy sequence into a concrete stored collection, such as a list, computing every element now.
example: list(map(f, xs)) materialises the map iterator.

definition: Processing data piece by piece as it arrives, so you never need to hold all of it in memory at once.
example: Reading a 50 GB log line by line and keeping only the first 10 matches is streaming.

definition: Building a description of a computation now and running it only when a result is requested. Spark, LINQ, Java Streams and Django QuerySets all use it.
example: A Django QuerySet doesn't hit the database until you iterate it.

definition: A distributed data-processing engine. Its transformations (map, filter) only build a plan; nothing runs on the cluster until an action such as count or collect asks for a result.
example: rdd.map(parse).filter(ok) schedules no tasks; rdd.count() does.

definition: Resilient Distributed Dataset: Spark's basic collection, split across a cluster and rebuilt from its lineage if a machine fails.
example: sc.textFile(path) creates an RDD of lines.

definition: A Spark operation, such as count, collect, take or saveAsTextFile, that asks for a result and so triggers execution of the deferred transformations.
example: rdd.count() is an action that runs the whole pipeline.

definition: A Spark operation, such as map or filter, that defines a new dataset from an old one without running anything yet.
example: rdd.map(parse) is a transformation; it returns immediately.

definition: The record of which transformations produce a Spark dataset from its sources. Spark uses it to plan the job and to recompute lost partitions.
example: read file → parse → filter is a three-step lineage.

definition: Language Integrated Query: C# and .NET query operators (Select, Where, SelectMany and more). Most queries use deferred execution, running only when enumerated, and re-running each time they are enumerated.
example: Iterating the same LINQ-to-database query twice can query the database twice.

definition: Java's java.util.stream API for pipelines of operations such as map and filter. Intermediate operations are lazy; nothing runs until a terminal operation such as collect or count.
example: list.stream().filter(x -> x > 0).count() runs the filter when count is called.

definition: In Java Streams, the final operation, such as collect, count or forEach, that produces a result and triggers the lazy pipeline to run.
example: collect(Collectors.toList()) is a terminal operation.

definition: Django's object-relational mapper, which turns Python method calls into SQL. Its QuerySets are lazy: building one doesn't touch the database, but iterating, len(), list(), bool() and some others run the query.
example: Entry.objects.filter(pub=True) runs no SQL until you loop over it.

definition: A fast DataFrame library for Python and Rust. Its lazy frames record a whole query and optimise it, for example pushing filters down, before executing.
example: pl.scan_csv("x.csv").filter(...).collect() runs an optimised plan.

definition: A query optimisation that applies filters as early as possible, ideally while reading data, so less data flows through later steps.
example: Filtering rows while scanning a file instead of after loading it all.

definition: Memory held much longer, or in much larger amounts, than the program needs, typically because unevaluated thunks pile up in a lazy language.
example: foldl (+) 0 [1..10^7] can hold ten million suspended additions.

definition: Haskell's primitive seq a b, which forces a to weak head normal form before returning b. It is how foldl' keeps its accumulator evaluated.
example: seq (undefined, 1) "ok" returns "ok", because the pair constructor is already in WHNF.

definition: An expression evaluated only as far as its outermost constructor or lambda, with its contents possibly still unevaluated thunks. seq forces values only this far.
example: (undefined, 1) is already in WHNF: it is visibly a pair.

definition: A Haskell library function that forces a value all the way down (to normal form) using the type's NFData instance, instead of stopping at weak head normal form like seq.
example: deepseq (undefined, 1) () crashes, while seq (undefined, 1) () does not.

definition: In Haskell, the tag that builds a value of a data type, such as (,) for pairs, : for non-empty lists or Just for Maybe. Weak head normal form stops once the outermost one is known.
example: (1, 2) is built by the pair constructor; x : xs by the list constructor :.

definition: The chain of cons cells (:) that gives a list its structure and length, as opposed to the elements stored in it. length walks the spine without evaluating the elements.
example: length [undefined, undefined] is 2, because only the spine is examined.

definition: A Haskell value that raises an error when it is forced. It is handy for testing laziness: an expression containing it succeeds only if that part is never evaluated.
example: fst (1, undefined) is 1.

definition: A GHC extension that marks a pattern variable with ! so it is forced to weak head normal form when the function is called.
example: go !acc (x:xs) = go (acc + x) xs keeps acc evaluated.

definition: A GHC language extension that makes bindings in a module strict by default, as if every pattern had a bang.
example: {-# LANGUAGE Strict #-} at the top of a file turns it on.

definition: Haskell's style of input where functions such as readFile return their content lazily, reading the file only as the data is demanded. The file handle can stay open far longer than expected.
example: readFile then writeFile to the same path can fail because the handle is still open.

definition: An operating-system resource representing an open file. Programs must close handles; a lazy reader can keep one open until all its data has been consumed.
example: with open(path) as f: closes the handle when the block ends.

definition: conduit and pipes are Haskell streaming libraries that process data incrementally with predictable resource use, as an alternative to lazy I/O.
example: A conduit pipeline can read a 10 GB file in constant memory.

definition: Haskell's module for strict, efficient Unicode text I/O, which reads files eagerly instead of lazily.
example: Data.Text.IO.readFile reads the whole file and closes it straight away.

definition: Opt-in laziness in JVM languages: Scala's LazyList (a lazily built list) and lazy val (a value computed on first use), and Kotlin's Sequence and by lazy, which do the same jobs.
example: Scala's lazy val config = load() runs load() only on first access.

definition: Short for "I owe you": a promise to pay later. It is a handy picture of a thunk, which promises a value it hasn't computed yet.
example: A thunk for slow_query() is an IOU for its result.

definition: A Haskell function that combines two lists element by element with a given function, stopping at the shorter list.
A type that supports a map operation which applies a function to the value or values inside it and keeps the surrounding structure. Lists, optionals and Promises are functors.
example: Some(3).map(x => x + 1) gives Some(4); [1, 2].map(x => x + 1) gives [2, 3].

definition: The two rules a lawful map must obey: mapping the identity function changes nothing, and mapping f then g equals mapping their composition once. They guarantee map only transforms contents.
example: map(id, [1, 2]) must equal [1, 2].

definition: The function that returns its argument unchanged, often written id: id(x) = x.
example: In Python, lambda x: x is the identity function.

definition: A type with two operations, one that wraps a plain value (return or pure) and one that chains a step returning another wrapped value (bind, flat_map), obeying three laws. The type decides what "and then" means: skip on missing, stop on error, try every option, or wait.
example: Maybe, Either, lists, IO and (roughly) Promises are monads.

definition: An informal picture used for functors and monads: a value packaged with some context, such as "might be missing", "might be an error", "many values" or "not here yet".
example: Some(3), Ok(3), [3] and Promise.resolve(3) all "box" the number 3.

definition: The monad operation that runs a box-returning function on the contents and keeps a single layer of box: map, then flatten. Haskell calls it bind and writes it >>=; Rust uses and_then, JavaScript arrays flatMap, LINQ SelectMany.
The monad operation that puts a plain value into a box with no extra effect: Some(x), Ok(x), [x] or Promise.resolve(x). Haskell names it return or pure; the lesson calls it wrap.
example: return 5 in the Maybe monad is Just 5.

definition: Three rules a lawful monad obeys: left identity (wrapping then binding f equals calling f), right identity (binding wrap changes nothing) and associativity (how binds are grouped doesn't matter). They make refactoring chains safe.
example: Some(2).flat_map(f) must equal f(2).

definition: The monad law wrap(x) >>= f = f(x): wrapping a value and then chaining f is the same as just calling f.
example: Some(2).flat_map(lambda x: Some(x + 1)) must be Some(3), the same as f(2).

definition: The monad law m >>= wrap = m: chaining the wrap function onto a box gives back the same box.
example: Some(5).flat_map(Some) is Some(5).

definition: The monad law (m >>= f) >>= g = m >>= (λx. f(x) >>= g): binding f then g gives the same result as binding one combined step. It is what lets you extract or inline helper functions in a chain.
example: m.flat_map(f).flat_map(g) equals m.flat_map(lambda x: f(x).flat_map(g)).

definition: A branch of mathematics about objects and the structure-preserving maps between them. Functors and monads come from it, but you can use them in code without knowing it.
example: In category theory a monad is defined by a unit and a join (flatten) operation.

definition: Haskell's optional type: a value is either Just x or Nothing. The lesson's Python Maybe class imitates it with Some(x) and Nothing.
example: lookup 3 [(1, "a")] returns Nothing.

definition: A type that holds either one value or nothing, making possible absence explicit: Java's Optional, Rust's Option, Swift's optionals. Its map and flatMap skip work when empty.
example: Optional.of(3).map(x -> x + 1) is Optional[4]; Optional.empty().map(...) stays empty.

definition: A type that holds either a success value (Ok) or an error (Err), so failures are visible in the return type. Rust uses it for recoverable errors; Haskell's equivalent is Either.
example: parse("abc") returns Err("not a number: abc").

definition: Haskell's two-case type: Left holds an error (by convention) and Right a success. As a monad it stops at the first Left.
example: Right 4 >>= (\n -> if n > 0 then Right n else Left "must be > 0") gives Right 4.

definition: A JavaScript object representing a value that will arrive later: it is pending, then fulfilled with a value or rejected with an error. then chains steps and automatically flattens a returned Promise.
example: fetch(url).then(r => r.json()) gives a Promise of the parsed body.

definition: The Promise method p.then(f), which runs f when p fulfils. If f returns a plain value the result is a Promise of it (like map); if f returns a Promise, then waits for it and flattens (like flat_map).
example: Promise.resolve(1).then(x => x + 1) is a Promise of 2.

definition: Any JavaScript object with a then method. Promises treat thenables like Promises and adopt their eventual value, which is how flattening works and why Promises break the left identity law.
example: { then(r) { r(42) } } is a thenable; awaiting it gives 42.

definition: Syntax in JavaScript, Python, C#, Rust and other languages for writing asynchronous code as straight-line statements: await pauses an async function until a Promise, future or task completes and gives its result, letting other work run meanwhile.
example: In JavaScript, const r = await fetch(url); waits for the response without blocking the event loop.

definition: The states of a JavaScript Promise: fulfilled (succeeded with a value), rejected (failed with a reason) or pending; "settled" means fulfilled or rejected.
example: Promise.reject(new Error("x")) is a rejected Promise.

definition: A small job JavaScript runs as soon as the current code finishes, before other events. Promise callbacks run as microtasks, so restructuring a then-chain can change when code runs.
example: Promise.resolve().then(f) schedules f as a microtask.

definition: JavaScript's ?. operator: a?.b gives undefined instead of throwing when a is null or undefined, and stops the rest of the chain.
example: user?.address?.city is undefined if user has no address.

definition: Rust's postfix ? on a Result or Option: it unwraps a success value, or returns the error (converted with From) or None from the enclosing function immediately.
example: let text = fs::read_to_string(p)?; returns early if reading fails.

definition: Stopping a chain of operations as soon as the outcome is decided, skipping the rest: and/or skipping their right side, or a Maybe chain stopping at the first Nothing.
example: In x is not None and x.ok, x.ok is never evaluated when x is None.

definition: LINQ's name for flat_map on sequences: it maps each element to a sequence and concatenates the results.
example: new[] {1, 2}.SelectMany(x => new[] {x, x}) gives 1, 1, 2, 2.

definition: Haskell syntax that writes a chain of monadic binds as a sequence of steps: x <- action binds the result of action to x. It is syntactic sugar for >>=.
example: do { u <- findUser 1; findTeam u } means findUser 1 >>= findTeam.

definition: Syntax that makes something easier to write or read but adds no new capability, because it translates directly into existing constructs.
example: Python's a[i] is syntactic sugar for a.__getitem__(i).

definition: Scala's for/yield syntax and F#'s computation expressions: syntax that, like Haskell's do-notation, writes chains of flatMap and map as sequential steps.
example: for { u <- findUser(1); t <- findTeam(u) } yield t chains two flatMaps.

definition: Haskell's type for actions that interact with the outside world. Its >>= sequences effects in order, so I/O stays explicit in the types of otherwise pure code.
example: getLine >>= putStrLn reads a line and prints it.

definition: Scott Wlaschin's picture of Result chaining as two tracks: each step runs on the success track, and the first failure switches to the error track, where later steps are skipped.
example: parse, then validate, then save: a parse error skips validate and save.

definition: A Haskell building block that stacks one monad's behaviour on top of another, such as error handling on top of I/O, so one chain handles both layers.
example: ExceptT Error IO a is IO with Either-style errors layered on.

definition: A Scala library for typed, composable effects, combining asynchronous code, errors and resources in one type so they chain together.
example: ZIO[Any, Error, User] describes an effect that fails with Error or succeeds with a User.

definition: A TypeScript library for typed effects that tracks success values, errors and requirements in one type, playing a role similar to ZIO in Scala.
example: Effect.Effect<User, NotFound> describes a computation that may fail with NotFound.

definition: A Java exception that a method must either handle or declare with throws, so the compiler forces callers to deal with it.
example: void load() throws IOException makes callers handle or rethrow IOException.

definition: An error signal that unwinds the call stack until some code catches it. Exceptions short-circuit a sequence of steps, but the possibility of failure does not usually appear in a function's return type.
example: int("x") raises ValueError, skipping the rest of the try block.

definition: A special value meaning "no object". Python calls it None, JavaScript has both null and undefined. Optional types make the possibility of absence explicit instead.
example: Java's Optional.map turns a null result into an empty Optional.

definition: Apple's programming language for iOS and macOS, with built-in optional types, optional chaining and a throws mechanism for declared errors.
example: user?.address?.city uses Swift optional chaining.

definition: A data structure where every update returns a new version while the old version stays valid and usable. Efficient ones share most of their memory between versions. "Persistent" here has nothing to do with disks.
example: After v2 = insert(v1, 65), both v1 and v2 can still be read.

definition: An ordinary mutable data structure, where an update destroys the previous version.
example: After xs.append(3) on a Python list, the old two-element version is gone.

definition: Persistence in which every old version can still be read, but only the newest can be updated.
example: A versioned document where you can view any old revision but only edit the latest.

definition: Persistence in which every version, old or new, can be both read and used as the starting point of further updates. Purely functional structures are fully persistent automatically.
example: Two different updates of the same old version of a map both work.

definition: Persistence in which versions can also be combined, so a new version can be made from two or more older ones, as in merging two lists.
example: Concatenating two old versions of a persistent list into a new one.

definition: Reusing the unchanged parts of a data structure between its old and new versions instead of copying them. It is what makes persistent updates cheap.
example: Two lists [1, 2, 3] and [9, 2, 3] can share the cells for [2, 3].

definition: A singly linked list built from cells that each hold one value and a pointer to the rest of the list. Prepending shares the old list, so it is the simplest persistent structure. Lisp, Haskell and Erlang lists are cons lists.
example: 1 : [2, 3] in Haskell creates one new cell pointing at [2, 3].

definition: Adding an element at the front of a list. On a cons list it is O(1): allocate one cell pointing at the existing list.
example: Prepending 9 to [2, 3] gives [9, 2, 3] and leaves [2, 3] intact.

definition: The head of a list is its first element; the tail is everything after it, itself a list. On a cons list both are one pointer away.
example: For [1, 2, 3] the head is 1 and the tail is [2, 3].

definition: The persistent-update technique for trees: copy only the nodes on the path from the root to the change, and reuse every subtree off that path by pointer.
example: Inserting 65 into the lesson's tree copies nodes 50, 70 and 60 and shares the rest.

definition: A tree kept so that all root-to-leaf paths have roughly the same length, giving a height of about log₂ n for n keys. Red-black and AVL trees rebalance automatically.
example: A balanced tree of a million keys is about 20 levels deep.

definition: A self-balancing binary search tree that colours each node red or black and enforces colour rules that keep its height within about twice the minimum.
example: Java's TreeMap is a red-black tree.

definition: A self-balancing binary search tree in which the heights of every node's two subtrees differ by at most one, restored by rotations after updates.
example: Inserting 1, 2, 3 into an AVL tree triggers a rotation that makes 2 the root.

definition: A local rearrangement of a few nodes in a binary search tree that changes its shape but not its order, used to rebalance it.
example: A left rotation makes a node's right child its parent.

definition: Haskell's standard persistent ordered map (and Data.Set its set counterpart) from the containers package, implemented as size-balanced binary trees with O(log n) updates.
example: Map.insert 3 "c" m returns a new map and leaves m unchanged.

definition: Scala's immutable sorted map, implemented as a persistent red-black tree.
example: TreeMap(3 -> "c", 1 -> "a") iterates in key order 1, 3.

definition: A version-control system that stores each commit as a snapshot made of content-addressed objects, sharing unchanged files and directories between commits.
example: git commit records a new snapshot that reuses every unchanged object.

definition: A Git object recording one snapshot of a project: a pointer to the root tree object, the parent commit(s), author and message.
example: Changing one file creates a new commit whose tree shares all unchanged directories with its parent.

definition: A Git object representing one directory: a list of names pointing to blobs (files) and other trees (subdirectories), each by hash.
example: Changing src/main.c creates new trees for src/ and the root, and reuses all other trees.

definition: A Git object storing the contents of one file, identified by the hash of that content.
example: Two identical files anywhere in a repository share one blob.

definition: An immutable indexed sequence stored as a wide trie with up to 32 children per node, used by Clojure, Scala and Immutable.js. Lookups and updates take about log₃₂ n steps, at most 6 for a billion elements.
example: Updating index 1000 of a million-element vector copies 4 small arrays.

definition: The maximum number of children a tree node has. A larger branching factor makes the tree shallower: 32 children per node give about log₃₂ n levels instead of log₂ n.
example: With a branching factor of 32, three levels hold 32,768 elements.

definition: In Clojure's persistent vector, a separate array holding the last (up to) 32 elements outside the trie, so most appends only copy that small array.
example: Appending to a vector of 40 elements copies its 8-element tail array.

definition: The inverse of raising to a power: log_b(n) is the power you raise b to in order to get n, which is roughly how many times you can divide n by b before reaching 1.
The function ⌈x⌉, which rounds a number up to the next whole number (whole numbers stay as they are).
Big-O notation for a cost that stays below a fixed bound however large the input is.
example: Reading the head of a cons list is O(1), whether it has 3 or 3 million elements.

definition: Big-O notation for a cost that grows with the logarithm of n, adding roughly a constant amount of work each time n doubles (or, for a 32-way trie, each time n grows 32-fold).
example: A balanced tree of a million keys needs about 20 steps; of two million, about 21.

definition: Big-O notation for a cost proportional to n times the logarithm of n, typical of efficient comparison sorting.
example: Sorting a million items takes on the order of 20 million comparisons.

definition: Big-O notation for a cost proportional to i, the position being reached, as when walking i pointers along a linked list.
example: Reading index 500 of a cons list walks 500 pointers.

definition: A persistent hash map or set: a 32-way trie indexed by successive 5-bit chunks of a key's hash, with bitmap nodes that store only occupied slots. Clojure, Scala, Immutable.js and CPython's contextvars use it.
example: A sparse HAMT node with 3 children stores 3 pointers plus a 32-bit bitmap.

definition: A sequence of bits used as a compact set of flags. In a HAMT node, bit k is 1 when slot k has a child.
example: The bitmap 0b10110 marks slots 1, 2 and 4 as occupied.

definition: The number of 1 bits in a binary number. HAMTs use it to turn a slot number into a position in a compact array; many processors have a single instruction for it.
example: popcount(0b00110) = 2.

definition: Two different keys producing the same hash value. Hash structures need a fallback for it; HAMTs use special collision nodes.
example: Two strings with identical 32-bit hashes collide in a HAMT and share a collision node.

definition: The key–value map type of Erlang and Elixir. Small maps (up to 32 keys) are stored as sorted arrays; larger ones as a HAMT.
example: #{a => 1} in Erlang or %{a: 1} in Elixir creates a map.

definition: A saved copy of a data structure's state at one moment. With persistent data, keeping a reference to the old root is a snapshot, at no copying cost.
example: An undo stack of 50 previous document versions is 50 snapshots.

definition: Making a newly built object visible to other threads in a way that guarantees they see it fully initialised, such as through a lock, a volatile field or an atomic reference.
example: Storing a new persistent map in a Clojure atom publishes it safely to readers.

definition: A Clojure reference that holds one immutable value and is updated atomically with swap!, which uses compare-and-set and retries if another thread changed it first.
example: (swap! counter inc) adds 1 to the value in the atom counter.

definition: An atomic processor operation that changes a memory location to a new value only if it still holds an expected old value. It lets threads update shared references without locks.
example: CAS(ptr, old, new) fails if another thread replaced old first, so the writer retries.

definition: The fixed multiplier that Big-O notation ignores. Two O(1) operations can still differ several-fold in real speed, such as one pointer load versus four.
example: A persistent vector lookup and an array lookup are both effectively O(1), but the array is faster.

definition: A value holding the memory address of another value. Following a chain of pointers (pointer chasing) is slow when each load must wait for the one before.
example: A 4-level trie lookup follows 4 pointers.

definition: The average cost per operation over any sequence of operations, which can be small even if some individual operations are expensive. Persistence can break amortised bounds when an expensive step is replayed from an old version.
example: A two-list queue does an occasional O(n) reverse but costs O(1) amortised per operation.

definition: A purely functional first-in, first-out queue made of two lists: push onto back, pop from front, and reverse back into front when front runs out.
example: Pushing 1, 2, 3 then popping gives 1 after one reverse of [3, 2, 1].

definition: A guarantee about the most expensive any single operation can be, stronger than an amortised bound, which only limits the average.
example: Okasaki's real-time queues give O(1) worst-case pushes and pops.

definition: Chris Okasaki's 1996 thesis and 1998 book on designing efficient immutable data structures, including combining laziness with persistence to keep amortised bounds.
example: Its banker's queue uses lazy evaluation so replayed pops share one reversal.

definition: A thunk that stores its result after the first evaluation, so every version of a persistent structure that shares it pays for the work only once.
example: Two branches of a search popping the same old queue share one memoised reversal.

definition: Temporary mutable versions of Clojure's persistent collections, made with transient and turned back with persistent! in O(1). They speed up bulk builds as long as no one else sees them while they change.
example: (persistent! (reduce conj! (transient []) (range 100000))) builds a vector quickly.

definition: An Immutable.js method that applies a batch of updates to a temporary mutable copy and returns a new immutable collection.
example: map.withMutations(m => { m.set("a", 1).set("b", 2) }) creates one new version, not two.

definition: A Python library of persistent collections with structural sharing: pvector is a 32-way vector trie, pmap is a hash table whose buckets live in a pvector, and pset is built on pmap. Lookups and updates take about log₃₂ n steps.
example: v2 = pvector([1, 2]).append(3) leaves the first vector unchanged.

definition: A Python tuple subclass with named fields, created with typing.NamedTuple. Its _replace method returns a new tuple with some fields changed.
example: Node(5, None, None)._replace(left=n) builds a new node.

definition: A stack of previous states (or reversible commands) that lets a user step back. With persistent data it can simply be a list of old values.
example: An editor keeping the last 100 document values as an undo stack.

definition: A binary digit, 0 or 1: the smallest unit of information.
example: A 5-bit chunk can hold 32 values, 0 to 31.

definition: A unit of data of a trillion bytes (10^12 B), a thousand gigabytes.
example: A 2 TB dataset is spread across many machines in a Spark cluster.

definition: Describes a processor or program whose addresses and registers are 64 bits wide, so a pointer takes 8 bytes.
example: On a 64-bit build of CPython each tuple slot is an 8-byte pointer.

definition: The creator of Clojure, who designed its persistent vector and hash map, building on Phil Bagwell's hash array mapped trie.
example: Clojure was first released in 2007.

definition: A computer scientist who invented the hash array mapped trie (2001), the basis of persistent hash maps in Clojure and Scala.
example: His paper "Ideal Hash Trees" introduced HAMTs.

definition: Joining two sequences end to end into a new one, such as [1, 2] + [3] in Python or xs ++ ys in Haskell. Python's + on lists and tuples copies the references from both sides into a new sequence; Haskell's ++ copies the cells of the left-hand list and shares the right-hand one. Either way it costs time in proportion to the length copied.
example: [1, 2] + [3] gives [1, 2, 3] and leaves both original lists unchanged.
